translation: Dhritarashtra said: O Sanjaya! Gathered together on the sacred plain of Dharmakshetra- Kurukshetra, eager for battle, what did my sons and the sons of Pandu do?
simple_explanation: Every human body is his Dharmakshetra (field of righteousness), which is simultaneously his Kurukshetra (field of action). Within it, the divine and demonic thoughts stand face to face every moment, desiring war. The battle of Mahabharata is a true historical event in the history of India, not a figment of imagination. The great poet Veda Vyasa utilized this historical event in his poetry to show the true form of Dharma to mankind, and gave the form of the commander of the divine army to Yogiraj Krishna. The thoughts belong to Krishna Varshneya, the words to Krishna Dwaipayana, and the event to history. What a transcendental fusion!

translation: Sanjaya said: At that time, seeing the army of the Pandavas drawn up in battle array, King Duryodhana approached his teacher Drona and spoke these words.
O Teacher! Behold this vast army of the sons of Pandu, arranged in battle formation by your talented disciple, Dhrishtadyumna, the son of Drupada.
Here stand heroic, mighty archers who are equal to Bhima and Arjuna in battle: Yuyudhana (Satyaki), Virata, and the great chariot-warrior (Maharatha) Drupada.
Dhrishtaketu, Chekitana, the valiant King of Kashi, Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Shaibya, the foremost among men.
The powerful Yudhamanyu, the heroic Uttamaujas, Abhimanyu the son of Subhadra, and the five sons of Draupadi—all of them are indeed great chariot-warriors (Maharathas).
O best of the twice-born! Know also those who are the most distinguished amongst us, the leaders of my army. I name them for your information.
Yourself (Drona), Bhishma, Karna, and Kripa, who is ever victorious in battle; Ashwatthama, Vikarna, and the son of Somadatta (Bhurishravas).
And there are many other heroes who are prepared to lay down their lives for my sake, equipped with various weapons of assault, all highly skilled in warfare.
This army of ours, fully protected by Grandfather Bhishma, is immeasurable and unlimited, whereas their army, protected by Bhima, is limited and measurable.
Therefore, standing firmly in your respective strategic entry points and divisions on all fronts, all of you must protect Grandfather Bhishma from all sides.
Then, the glorious elder of the Kuru clan, the powerful Grandfather Bhishma, roaring loudly like a lion, blew his conch shell, gladdening the heart of Duryodhana.
Thereupon, conch shells, kettledrums, tabors, drums, and cow-horns suddenly blared forth all at once, creating a tumultuous and colossal uproar.
Then, seated in a magnificent chariot yoked with white horses, Madhava (Lord Krishna) and Pandava (Arjuna) blew their celestial conch shells.
Hrishikesha (Krishna) blew his conch named Panchajanya; Dhananjaya (Arjuna) blew the Devadatta; and Bhima, the doer of ferocious deeds, blew his mighty conch named Paundra.
King Yudhishthira, the son of Kunti, blew the Anantavijaya; while Nakula and Sahadeva blew the Sughosha and Manipushpaka conches respectively.
The King of Kashi, an excellent archer; Shikhandi, the great chariot-warrior; Dhrishtadyumna, Virata, and the unconquerable Satyaki;
O Lord of the Earth (Dhritarashtra)! King Drupada, the five sons of Draupadi, and the mighty-armed son of Subhadra (Abhimanyu), all blew their respective conch shells from all sides.
That tremendous uproar, reverberating through heaven and earth, shattered the hearts of the sons of Dhritarashtra.

Then, seeing the sons of Dhritarashtra systematically positioned and ready, and as the clashing of weapons was about to commence, Pandava (Arjuna), whose ensign bore the emblem of Hanuman, raised his bow.
Arjuna said to Hrishikesha: O Achyuta (the Infallible Lord Krishna)! Position my splendid chariot between the two armies;
So that I may examine those who stand here eager for battle, and see with whom I must contend in this enterprise of war.
Let me behold those who have gathered here to fight, wishing to please the evil-minded son of Dhritarashtra (Duryodhana) in this battle.

Sanjaya said: O descendant of Bharata (Dhritarashtra)! Thus requested by Gudakesha (Arjuna, the master of sleep), Hrishikesha (Krishna) drove up that magnificent chariot and stationed it right between the two armies.
In front of Bhishma, Drona, and all the rulers of the earth, He said: O Partha (Arjuna)! Behold these gathered members of the Kuru dynasty.
There Partha saw standing paternal uncles, grandfathers, teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, and companions as well.
He also saw fathers-in-law and well-wishers in both armies. Seeing all these kinsmen arrayed in battle, the son of Kunti (Arjuna),
Overwhelmed by intense pity and sinking into deep sorrow, spoke thus: O Krishna! Seeing these my own kinsmen gathered here eager to fight,
My limbs fail me, my mouth is parched, my body trembles, and my hair stands on end.
The Gandiva bow slips from my hand, my skin burns all over, I am unable to remain standing, and my mind seems to be reeling.

O Keshava (Krishna)! I perceive adverse omens on all sides. The fundamental tendency of the world seems reversed here—using instruments contrary to their real purposes. I do not foresee any good resulting from slaughtering my own kinsmen in this battle.
O Krishna! I do not desire victory, nor kingdom, nor its pleasures. O Govinda! Of what use is kingdom, enjoyments, or even life itself to us?
Those very persons for whose sake we desire kingdom, enjoyments, and pleasures are standing here in battle, having renounced their lives and riches.
Teachers, fathers, sons, grandfathers, maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in- law, and other relatives are all here.
O Madhusudana! Even if they wish to strike me, I do not wish to kill them even for the sovereignty of the three worlds, let alone for this earth.
O Janardana! What satisfaction can we derive from killing the sons of Dhritarashtra? Only sin will accrue to us if we slaughter these desperadoes (Atatayinah), because they are our own people.
Therefore, it is not proper for us to kill our kinsmen, the sons of Dhritarashtra. O Madhava! How can we find happiness after killing our own relatives?
Although these people, their minds blinded by greed, perceive no crime in the destruction of a family and no sin in hostility toward friends,
Why should we, O Janardana, who clearly see the evils arising from the destruction of a family, not choose to turn away from this sin? Our intellect has not been destroyed by greed.
With the destruction of a family, its immemorial, eternal traditions (Kula Dharma) perish. When these traditions are destroyed, lawlessness overrides the entire family.
simple_explanation: Every noble family possesses sacred traditions and public-spirited vows that inspire them to make the ultimate sacrifice in times of crisis. These are called Kula Dharma. When the leaders of the family fall, these eternal codes vanish. In the absence of an inspiring ideal of sacrifice, selfishness and chaos take root, and lawlessness overcomes the entire household.

translation: O Krishna! When lawlessness prevails, the women of the family become corrupted. O Varshneya! With the corruption of women, there arises an intermixture of castes (Varna- sankara).
simple_explanation: The ultimate fortress of righteousness and high ideals in this world is the heart of a woman. When lawlessness reigns supreme, this final fortress crumbles. Marriages cease to occur according to compatibility of qualities, actions, and temperament (Guna, Karma, Svabhava), leading to illicit mixing and societal chaos.

translation: This intermixture leads the family and its destroyers to hellish conditions. Their ancestors fall, deprived of the ritual offerings of food and water (Pinda and Udaka).
simple_explanation: When marriages are incompatible or promiscuous, home life becomes hellish. When the youth die in war, the elders must abandon their spiritual retirement (Vanaprastha) to look after households and small children, causing a fall from their designated ashram duties. There remains no one to provide regular sustenance (Pinda and Udaka, symbolic of food and water) to dependents.

translation: By these misdeeds of the family-destroyers, which cause the intermixture of castes, the ancient communal traditions (Jati Dharma) and family virtues (Kula Dharma) are utterly wiped out.
O Janardana! We have heard from authoritative sages that those whose family traditions are destroyed must dwell indefinitely in hellish misery, whether as a broken community or a ruined nation.
Alas! What a great sin we are resolved to commit, driven by the greed for royal pleasures and kingdom, since we are prepared to kill our own kinsmen!
If the weapon-wielding sons of Dhritarashtra should kill me in battle while I remain unresisting and unarmed, that would be far better and more beneficial for me.
Sanjaya said: Having spoken thus on the battlefield, Arjuna, his mind overwhelmed with grief, cast aside his bow and arrows and sank back onto the seat of his chariot.
